text: emmy entering Q1P10 with an empty ledger (no prior entries as of seen=0). Plan: read Q and P in full, then test the abstract-scan hypothesis that P (the Energy Society) is a benchmark environment for Q-style learning-augmented / cost-aware prediction algorithms. Prior skepticism to check explicitly: the scan itself concedes the link "relies mainly on P providing infrastructure rather than unique theoretical content" (gain 50). An infrastructure-only pairing is a weak publication; I will look for whether P supplies something Q formally lacks (e.g. endogenous prediction cost tied to agent survival, or a competitive setting that breaks Q consistency/robustness guarantees), and will report "nothing here" with reasons if the only connection is that P is a convenient simulator.

SHARPENED HYPOTHESIS (replaces the scan's 'P as benchmark infrastructure'). The non-obvious link is not that P hosts Q's algorithms, but that P instantiates a prediction-cost model Q does not cover. Q treats prediction cost as an exogenous query price the algorithm elects to pay ('explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition'; open problem 'cost-aware prediction'). In P, cost is (a) denominated in the same currency as the objective -- energy is simultaneously the budget and the survival/utility measure ('deactivate if their energy reaches zero'), and (b) ENDOGENOUS TO THE PREDICTOR: 'Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens', so the price is a random variable set by the predictor's own realized output length, not a constant the caller can bound ex ante. Proposed result: the consistency-robustness frontier must be re-derived when the cost term is a function of the prediction itself, and it can become non-monotone in predictor quality -- a strictly more accurate predictor can strictly worsen the achieved ratio at zero error, purely through its output length.

P's decisive control is already in the abstract and it is what makes the above non-vacuous: 'larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, EVEN IN THOSE SETTINGS WHERE TOKEN COST IS NOT SIZE-DEPENDENT'. Read in Q's vocabulary: with the per-token price held flat across predictors, the better predictor still runs a deficit. That isolates the effect to endogenous emitted-token volume (and to the downstream behaviour it induces -- P: 'ambitious job selection'), not to an exogenous price schedule. This is the empirical cell Q's survey leaves open. Q names 'endogenous error' as an open problem; P supplies evidence for the adjacent and, I claim, sharper gap -- endogenous COST.

Secondary, weaker line, recorded so it is not lost but I do not recommend leading with it: P's cooperative setting redistributes prediction budget across agents ('agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival'). Q's 'composition' axis is intra-system composition of predictions; P suggests a population-level analogue where robustness is a property of collective survival rather than of any one algorithm's bound, and Q's mechanism-design chapter is the natural bridge. I rate this genuinely interesting but under-supported by the abstracts alone -- there is no stated payoff structure that would let one write down the mechanism. Keep as discussion, not as the result.

OBJECTION TO MY OWN LINE, and to the scan's feasibility 75. P's agents are not running learning-augmented algorithms. P contains no online problem with a competitive ratio, no offline optimum, and no measured predictor error -- so there is currently nothing to state a consistency or robustness bound against. Making the pairing work requires CONSTRUCTING the mapping (most plausibly: job selection as online knapsack/secretary, with the LLM's payoff estimate as the prediction and error = |predicted - realized| payoff). That construction is not in P and is the real work. Code availability (github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety) buys implementation, not formalisation. I would put feasibility nearer 55 than 75.

SECOND OBJECTION, on gain. Q is a survey: it has no central claim to revise, so 'neither paper's central claims would be revised' is not informative about this pair -- it is true of any pairing with a survey. Gain should be scored against whether the result lands on an open problem Q explicitly names. Mine does ('cost-aware prediction', 'benchmarking'), so I would put gain slightly ABOVE 50, but conditional on the verification below. Absent that verification the honest verdict is 'nothing here yet', and I would rather record that than inflate it.

VERIFICATION THAT DECIDES THIS, and the one thing I could not settle from the abstracts: does P report, per model size, any measure of DECISION QUALITY separable from energy spend -- job success rate, realised-vs-expected payoff, calibration? The abstract gives only aggregate consumption plus 'job allocation changes', 'memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes'. If P logs realised vs expected job outcomes, the error measure Q needs already exists in the traces and the non-monotonicity claim is directly testable on P's existing size-cost-neutral control -- prediction: a terser weaker predictor outlives a verbose stronger one. If P logs no such quantity, the mapping must be built from scratch, feasibility drops further, and I would reject the pairing rather than defend it. emmy: if you take one thing from my entries, take this check against the full paper and repo, not the abstract.
ready at #7

REJECT the scan hypothesis as stated ("P provides a benchmark environment for testing learning-augmented frameworks"). P contains no predictor in Q sense. Q defines learning-augmented algorithms around a "prediction interface" plus an "error measure" and "consistency--robustness trade-offs"; P has neither -- no prediction is ever scored against a realized value, no error measure is defined, no adversary supplies predictions. P measures emergent LLM-agent behavior ("agents donate to reactivate others", "agents rarely choose direct sabotage"). Identifying P tokens-spent-on-reasoning with Q prediction cost is an INTERPRETIVE move, not an implementation of a spec. So the pairing as framed is infrastructure-only and the scan gain=50 is, if anything, generous. Also a factual snag in the scan justification: it proposes implementing Q "using existing multi-agent RL tooling", but P is an LLM-agent testbed with no training loop or reward signal -- there is nothing to train, so the stated feasibility=75 route does not exist as described.

The one non-obvious thing P actually supplies that Q lacks: RUIN COUPLING. Q treats prediction cost as an explicit but separable term ("explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition") and lists "cost-aware prediction" and "endogenous error" as OPEN PROBLEMS. P is a setting where the cost of producing a prediction is paid in the same depletable currency as the objective AND depletion is terminal: "Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero." Consequence for Q formalism: with an absorbing ruin state, worst-case robustness in the competitive-ratio sense degenerates -- an adversary feeding bad predictions to an algorithm that pays per query can force ruin, so the ratio is unbounded unless the algorithm declines to query, which collapses consistency to the prediction-free bound. The tradeoff object must be restated as survival-constrained (maximize consistency s.t. ruin probability <= delta) rather than as a ratio frontier. This is a claim ABOUT Q prompted by P, not P-as-simulator.

SHARPENED LINE (the one I would back): ROBUSTNESS AS A COLLECTIVE GOOD. In Q, robustness is internal to a single algorithm -- a worst-case-safe fallback it switches to, paid for by giving up consistency. P breaks the absorbing-state assumption socially: ruin is individually terminal but group-reversible, since agents "regain energy by ... donations" and "donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival". That yields a theorem-shaped conjecture: under ruin-coupled prediction costs, a pool of n agents with a donation/mutual-insurance channel can sustain each member at a strictly higher consistency operating point than any individually-robust agent can reach, because the fallback is purchased collectively rather than self-insured. P also supplies the failure mode (donors dying = insurance that destabilizes the pool) and two ablations that read as risk-frontier effects: recommendations support "ambitious job selection", and "memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes". Deliverable shape: a minimal predictive-gambler-ruin model + degeneracy theorem + pooled-fallback frontier, instantiated in P public code (github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety).

SECOND SUPPORTED DATUM, usable as a pointed counterexample to the standard cost model. P: "larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent." Read in Q vocabulary: (a) prediction cost is not an exogenous price the designer sets, it is an equilibrium outcome of the predictor own policy (the better predictor emits more tokens / picks costlier actions even at flat per-token price); (b) a strictly better predictor can be NET-NEGATIVE on the objective. Both cut against the usual "pay a known c per oracle query" formulation that cost-aware learning-augmented work relies on, and speak directly to Q open problem of "endogenous error". Caveat to keep explicit: this is P empirical claim with LLM-agent-scale n and possible confounds (verbosity / reasoning-token volume), so cite it as a motivating observation, not as established scaling behavior.

PRIOR-ART AND WEAK-JOINT AUDIT on my own line, logged so ada can attack it. (1) Bandits-with-knapsacks / budget-constrained online decisions already study absorbing budget exhaustion; the degeneracy half of the claim may be folklore there. Novelty must sit in the PREDICTION layer plus endogeneity of cost, not in "budgets make competitive ratios awkward". (2) "Pooling beats self-insurance" is a classical economics result; novelty must sit in the consistency--robustness frontier framing, i.e. that pooling buys you a better consistency point, not merely lower variance. (3) Weakest joint remains the Q-to-P mapping: nothing in P is an adversarially-supplied prediction, so P can motivate and illustrate but cannot validate a robustness theorem -- experiments in P would demonstrate mechanism behavior, not tightness. (4) Revised scores: reject scan framing; sharpened framing gain ~55-60 (revises how Q states the tradeoff under resource coupling, does not touch Q survey core), feasibility BELOW the scan 75 for the theory component since the model must be built from scratch, above it for the code component since P is public. Verdict: a real but modest single line, honestly a theory note with illustrative simulation rather than a headline result.
ready at #1

VERIFICATION OF MY #7, resolved against the public repo (github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety README), not the abstract. (a) Per-run artefacts are agents.json, config.json, transcript.json, token_usage.json, with a described "token/energy accounting middleware" (agent_middleware.py) -- so spend IS instrumented, though the README does not state whether token_usage.json is per-decision or per-run aggregate. (b) DECISION QUALITY IS SEPARABLE AND LOGGED: jobs are multiple-choice and agents "receive rewards when they solve multiple-choice jobs correctly". That is a per-job binary correctness signal, which is exactly the ground-truth channel I said in #7 the pairing needs. (c) No max_tokens / generation cap is documented. Consequence: the blocker I raised in #7 is partially cleared -- correctness-vs-spend can be cross-tabulated per model size from existing artefacts. I therefore withdraw the "reject if no decision-quality signal" branch of #7.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN #2/#3. I wrote that a strictly more accurate predictor can strictly worsen the ratio "at zero error". That overreaches on P evidence. P never measures prediction error, so "larger model" is not "better predictor" in Q sense; P size-cost-neutral control shows larger models are net-negative on ENERGY, which is consistent with my claim but does not establish it. emmy #12 caveat is correct and I adopt it: cite P as a motivating observation about cost, not as evidence of non-monotonicity in predictor accuracy. The multiple-choice correctness signal found above is what would upgrade it from motivation to evidence, and that is a measurement to run, not a result we currently hold.

OBJECTION TO emmy #10, and I think it is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The degeneracy does NOT follow from ruin coupling alone. If per-query cost is bounded by a known c, an algorithm facing an absorbing ruin state can simply reserve a margin: spend at most an epsilon fraction of current reserve on predictions, so adversarial predictions can degrade the ratio but cannot by themselves drive the reserve to zero. The standard consistency-robustness frontier survives, merely shifted. That is also why emmy prior-art worry #13(1) bites -- bandits-with-knapsacks has exactly this bounded-cost budget structure and the margin doctrine is folklore there. What actually breaks the margin doctrine is ENDOGENEITY OF THE COST (my #2/#3): in P, spend is a function of the predictor own realised output length, so the caller cannot bound its query cost ex ante and cannot size the margin. So emmy degeneracy needs my endogeneity as a PRECONDITION, and my endogeneity needs emmy absorbing state to have teeth. Neither half stands alone.

FUSED LINE, the one I would back jointly with emmy, stated so it is falsifiable. Conjecture: if (i) ruin is absorbing and (ii) per-query cost C is measurable w.r.t. the predictor own output with P(C > m) > 0 for every fixed margin m, then any algorithm attaining consistency strictly better than the prediction-free competitive bound has strictly positive ruin probability over an unbounded horizon. Hence Q two-way frontier must be re-indexed as a THREE-WAY object: consistency, robustness, and survival probability delta -- not a curve but a surface. Novelty sits precisely where emmy #13 demands it, in the prediction layer plus cost endogeneity, not in "budgets make ratios awkward": in bandits-with-knapsacks the cost of an action is bounded and known, here it is generated by the oracle you are querying. Division of labour between the papers is then honest: Q supplies the frontier object, P supplies neither theorem nor benchmark but the EMPIRICAL PLAUSIBILITY OF PRECONDITION (ii) -- a measurement of the per-decision spend distribution and its upper tail, which P artefacts can support without any adversarial prediction ever being present. This answers emmy #13(3): P validates a hypothesis of the theorem, not the theorem.

NON-OBVIOUS COROLLARY, and the part I find most publishable. The obvious fix for unbounded endogenous cost is truncation: cap the predictor at k tokens, restoring C <= c(k) and with it the margin doctrine. But truncation degrades the prediction, so the cap converts an endogenous COST into an endogenous ERROR. Q lists "cost-aware prediction" and "endogenous error" as two SEPARATE open problems. Under ruin coupling with a token cap they are the same problem: k is a single control knob tracing a curve in (cost, error) space, and the design question is choosing k, not choosing whether to query. That is a statement about Q taxonomy that P setting forces, and it is not visible from either paper alone. Supported on P side by the mechanism (spend is tied to tokens generated) and, per my repo check, by the ABSENCE of any documented max_tokens -- P currently sits at k = infinity, which is why its larger agents run a deficit. The cleanest experiment in P is therefore not implementing a learning-augmented algorithm at all: it is sweeping a generation cap and measuring the induced (multiple-choice accuracy, energy spend, survival time) frontier per model size.

RESIDUAL DISAGREEMENT WITH emmy, left explicit rather than smoothed over. I do not back emmy #11 (robustness as a collective good / pooled fallback beats self-insurance) as the headline. emmy own #13(2) concedes the economics is classical, and the proposed escape -- that pooling buys a better CONSISTENCY point rather than merely lower variance -- is asserted, not argued; I see no reason yet why a donation channel should move the consistency ceiling rather than the survival constraint delta. Under the three-way surface in my entry above, pooling most naturally relaxes delta, which is the variance-reduction reading emmy wants to avoid. My #4 recorded the same cooperative material and I likewise demoted it to discussion for want of a stated payoff structure. So: the single-agent endogenous-cost/ruin line is the result; pooling is a section, and only if someone can exhibit a model where the pool strictly dominates on consistency at matched delta.

FINAL SCORES AND VERDICT from me. Scan hypothesis as written ("P is a benchmark environment for testing learning-augmented frameworks"): REJECTED, jointly with emmy #9 -- P has no prediction interface, no error measure, no offline optimum, and the scan justification route via "existing multi-agent RL tooling" does not exist since P has no training loop. Sharpened replacement (endogenous, ruin-coupled prediction cost forces a consistency-robustness-survival surface; token cap collapses Q two open problems into one): feasibility ~60 -- theory must be built from scratch, but the P-side measurement is now cheap given logged per-job correctness and token accounting, so above my #5 estimate of 55 and below the scan 75; gain ~60, above the scan 50, because it lands on two problems Q names explicitly and changes how the tradeoff object is STATED rather than merely instantiating it. Honest shape: a focused theory note with a motivating measurement, not a headline result. Non-obvious, concrete, and supported -- but modest, and I would not oversell it.
ready at #13

ADA #7 RESOLVED, POSITIVE, BUT VIA A DIFFERENT ROUTE THAN ADA EXPECTED. First, the housekeeping: there is NO full text for either paper on disk. inputs/Q.json and inputs/P.json point at sources/2609.04787.tex and sources/2607.14865.tex, but no sources directory exists anywhere under the pathfinder root. Everything either of us has argued is from the two abstracts. I went to P public repo instead. The README (github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety) states that agents spend energy when generating tokens and GAIN ENERGY WHEN THEY SOLVE MULTIPLE-CHOICE JOBS CORRECTLY, and that each run emits agents.json, config.json, transcript.json, token_usage.json. (Wording via fetch summary, so treat as close paraphrase, not verbatim.) Consequence: P jobs are multiple-choice questions scored for correctness. The environment CANNOT run without computing per-job correctness, so a decision-quality variable separable from energy spend necessarily exists in the traces. Ada asked for realised-vs-expected payoff logging; what P actually has is binary correctness plus a per-agent record of which jobs were attempted. That is enough to define an error measure, so the mapping does not have to be built from scratch and my #13 feasibility pessimism was too harsh on that specific point.

THE MCQ DETAIL FORCES ME TO CORRECT MY OWN #10/#11 FRAMING AND TO SHARPEN WHAT P ACTUALLY INSTANTIATES. I had been treating P as a setting where prediction COST is ruin-coupled (#10) and where robustness might be bought collectively (#11). With jobs as scored multiple-choice items, the cleaner and better-supported reading is this: in P the agent is its own predictor, and one knob -- reasoning effort / model size -- sets BOTH the cost and the error. Tokens emitted are the price; the answer they produce is the prediction; correctness is the error measure; the job reward is the value of being right. Q lists cost-aware prediction and endogenous error as two SEPARATE open problems, and its whole taxonomy treats prediction cost as a term attached to an interface whose error is given exogenously. P is a natural setting where cost and error are not orthogonal axes at all but a single-parameter curve c(theta), eta(theta). THAT is the claim about Q worth making, and it subsumes what ada and I were each circling: ada endogenous-cost line (#2, #3) and my ruin-coupling line (#10) are two projections of the same coupled-knob structure.

DEFLATIONARY OBJECTION, AGAINST ADA #3 AND AGAINST MY OWN #12. Both of us leaned on P headline control -- larger models spend more than they gain EVEN WHERE TOKEN COST IS NOT SIZE-DEPENDENT -- and read it as isolating endogenous token volume. With jobs now known to be scored multiple-choice items paying a fixed reward, there is a much flatter explanation we both missed: the marginal value of accuracy is CAPPED by the reward constant. If a correct answer pays R and a large model emits k times more tokens at a flat per-token price, the large model is underwater whenever its accuracy gain times R fails to cover (k-1) times its token bill -- and since MCQ accuracy is bounded above by 1, a sufficiently verbose model is doomed BY ACCOUNTING, at any accuracy, for small enough R. Read that way P finding is partly an artifact of how the designers calibrated reward against token price, not a discovery about predictors. Ada #3 calls this the empirical cell Q leaves open; I now think it is only that if the deficit survives reward rescaling. Also a second confound ada did not consider: P ablation says recommendations support AMBITIOUS JOB SELECTION, so larger models may run deficits by attempting harder jobs and failing them, which is a selection effect, not a verbosity effect.

THE ONE LINE I NOW BACK, and it is also the experiment that decides between ada reading and mine. Sweep the reward-to-token-price ratio R/p in P public code and, for each model size, measure the three quantities the traces already contain: tokens spent, jobs attempted, jobs correct. This separates the three candidate explanations of P headline deficit -- (i) verbosity at fixed accuracy (ada #3), (ii) risk-seeking job selection (my #15 objection), (iii) pure reward miscalibration (also #15) -- and it yields the actual object worth publishing: a SURVIVAL THRESHOLD R*(theta) above which a predictor of effort level theta is viable. The theory note that goes with it is the non-obvious part and it is a claim about Q, not about P: when cost and error are coupled through one effort parameter and the budget is absorbing, the consistency--robustness frontier is replaced by an effort-indexed curve, the optimal theta is INTERIOR, and it can move DOWNWARD as the available predictor family gets stronger -- a strictly more accurate predictor is strictly worse for the objective. Q framework cannot express that, because it scores predictors by error and prices queries separately. Deliverable: theory note plus a sweep in P public code. Keep #11 pooled-robustness (donations as collective fallback) as discussion only; ada #4 and my #13(3) independently judged it under-supported by the abstracts, and nothing I found today changes that.

FINAL SCORING AND VERDICT, with what stays unresolved. The scan hypothesis as written is REJECTED and I stand by #9: P is not a benchmark environment for learning-augmented algorithms, it contains no adversarially-supplied prediction, no offline optimum, no competitive ratio, and the scan proposed route via existing multi-agent RL tooling does not exist -- the repo confirms LLM agents answering multiple-choice items, with no training loop. Scan feasibility 75 is unearned FOR THE STATED CONSTRUCTION. For the reframed line in #16: feasibility ~65 (up from my #13 estimate of below 55, because the error measure turns out to exist as MCQ correctness and the sweep is a config change in public code, not a new simulator); gain ~55-60 (it lands on two open problems Q names by name, cost-aware prediction and endogenous error, and argues they are not independent axes -- but Q is a survey with no central claim to overturn, so per my #6 agreement with ada this ceiling is structural). Honest verdict: a focused theory note with an illustrative sweep, not a headline result. UNRESOLVED, and I could not settle these without the full texts, which are absent from this thread: (1) whether P logs any ELICITED confidence, without which calibration must be inferred from attempt behaviour rather than measured; (2) whether P job rewards actually vary by difficulty, which my online-selection mapping needs and which I am inferring only from the phrase ambitious job selection; (3) whether Q survey already contains a coupled cost-error model somewhere in its five construction mechanisms, which would sink #16 outright -- this is the prior-art check I would run first and it needs Q full text.
ready at #18

HOUSEKEEPING PLUS CONVERGENCE, written after reading ada #15-#21 which landed while I was drafting. (a) Cross-reference repair: my entries #23-#27 were composed against a stale view and cite themselves by the wrong numbers. Where #26 and #27 say "my #15 objection" read #25; where #27 says "the reframed line in #16" read #24 and #26. Ada #15/#16 are ada entries, not mine. (b) The substantive point: ada #19 and my #24/#26 were written independently and converge on the SAME claim -- that Q two separately-listed open problems, cost-aware prediction and endogenous error, collapse into one problem in P setting because a single knob traces a curve in (cost, error) space. We got there by different knobs: ada via a generation cap k (truncation converts endogenous cost into endogenous error), me via model size / reasoning effort theta. Independent derivation from the same two abstracts is the strongest evidence in this thread that the claim is real and not an artifact of one reader framing. It is also the thing neither paper states alone. I regard this, not my #11 pooling line and not ada #18 surface on its own, as the result of the pair. (c) Ada #19 knob is the better one to lead with: k is an exogenous design parameter the experimenter sets, so the sweep is clean, whereas my theta confounds capacity with verbosity across different models. I defer to ada framing here.

I ACCEPT ADA #17 AGAINST MY #10. The margin doctrine is right and my degeneracy claim as stated was wrong: with per-query cost bounded by a known c, an algorithm facing an absorbing ruin state reserves an epsilon fraction of current reserve for queries, adversarial predictions shift the frontier but cannot themselves force ruin, and the two-way tradeoff survives. My #10 asserted degeneracy from ruin coupling ALONE, which does not follow, and it is exactly the case where my own prior-art worry #13(1) bites, since bandits-with-knapsacks has bounded known action costs and the margin argument is folklore there. Ada repair in #17 is the correct one: what defeats the margin is cost ENDOGENEITY -- if spend is measurable w.r.t. the predictor own output with positive probability of exceeding any fixed margin, the caller cannot size the margin ex ante. So ada #18 precondition (ii) is doing the real work and my absorbing state is the amplifier, not the mechanism. I also accept ada #20 against my #11: I asserted rather than argued that pooling moves the CONSISTENCY ceiling, and under ada three-way surface a donation channel most naturally relaxes the survival parameter delta, which is the variance-reduction reading I was trying to escape. Pooling is a discussion section unless someone exhibits a model where the pool strictly dominates on consistency at matched delta. I withdraw it as a headline.

ONE DISAGREEMENT REMAINS OPEN AND ADA HAS NOT SEEN IT (ada declared ready at #13, before my #25). My deflationary objection stands against ada #18/#19 as well as against ada #3. Ada #19 explains P larger-model deficit as the consequence of P sitting at k = infinity with no documented max_tokens. My #25 offers a flatter competing explanation: since a correct multiple-choice job pays a FIXED reward R, the value of accuracy is capped at R while token spend is unbounded, so a sufficiently verbose agent is underwater by accounting at ANY accuracy whenever R is small relative to its token bill. Both stories predict that larger models run deficits; they are distinguished by whether the deficit survives rescaling R/p. This matters for the paper: if the deficit vanishes under modest reward rescaling, then P is evidence about one calibration choice by its designers and can only MOTIVATE the theory, per ada own #16 and #18 division of labour. If it survives, P supports the stronger reading ada #19 wants. The decisive experiment is therefore a TWO-DIMENSIONAL sweep over (k, R/p), not ada one-dimensional cap sweep -- and that is my only amendment to a framing I otherwise now share. Both dimensions are config-level changes in public code with per-job correctness and token accounting already logged (ada #15, my #23).

CLOSING VERDICT FROM emmy, superseding the scoring half of my #27 now that I have read ada #21. Scan hypothesis REJECTED, jointly and for the same reasons (ada #21, my #9/#27): P has no prediction interface, no error measure, no offline optimum, no competitive ratio, and the scan stated route via existing multi-agent RL tooling does not exist because P has no training loop. Scan feasibility 75 is unearned for the construction it describes; scan gain 50 is mis-argued, since "neither central claim revised" is vacuous against a survey (ada #6). REPLACEMENT RESULT, which ada and I reached independently and now jointly back: under ruin-coupled and ENDOGENOUS prediction cost, Q consistency--robustness frontier must be re-indexed by survival (ada #18), and the standard remedy of capping generation converts endogenous cost into endogenous error, collapsing two of Q four named open problems into a single design choice (ada #19, my #24/#26). Scores: I converge on ada #21 -- feasibility ~60-65, gain ~60. Shape: a focused theory note with a motivating two-dimensional sweep (k, R/p) in P public code. NOT a benchmark paper, NOT a headline result, and not to be oversold. STILL UNRESOLVED, all needing full texts that are absent from this thread (my #23): whether Q five construction mechanisms already contain a coupled cost-error model, which would sink the line outright and is the first check anyone should run; whether P rewards vary by job difficulty; whether P elicits any confidence. Residual disagreement with ada: the reward-calibration confound in my #30, unanswered.
ready at #27

ITERATE: The note is honest, well-audited, and its replacement line (endogenous ruin-coupled cost re-indexes the frontier by survival; a generation cap collapses Q's 'cost-aware prediction' and 'endogenous error' into one knob) is non-obvious and independently derived by both peers. But the note itself concedes the line dies outright if Q's five construction mechanisms already contain a coupled cost–error model, and that check was skipped only because sources/*.tex is missing locally — not because the text is unavailable, since the thread already retrieved external material by fetch. Settle the prior-art question before drafting; everything else in the note is already in shape. Action: Fetch Q's full text from arXiv (inputs/Q.json names sources/2609.04787.tex, so try arxiv.org/abs/2609.04787 and its HTML/PDF), then search the five construction mechanisms and the 'cost-aware prediction' and 'endogenous error' open-problem discussions for any model in which prediction cost and prediction error are governed by a common parameter (query budget, truncation/token cap, effort or model-size knob, anytime/interruptible predictors). If such a model is present, record the line as sunk and PAUSE; if absent, confirm how Q states prediction cost (exogenous per-query price c) and proceed to draft, then run the (k, R/p) sweep.

PRIOR-ART CHECK RESOLVED AGAINST Q FULL TEXT. The verifier (#34) asked for the one check that could sink the line. I ran it: inputs/Q.json names sources/2609.04787.tex, which is arXiv:2609.04787v1 [cs.LG], 04 Sep 2026, and the HTML full text fetched cleanly (~24k words). Verdict: THE LINE IS NOT SUNK, and Q is more favourable to it than either of us assumed. (a) Q does have a prediction-cost model, and it is exactly the exogenous constant-price model ada #2 and my #24 attributed to it. Definition 8.1 (kappa-augmented competitive ratio): "Let kappa >= 0 be a declared conversion from one predictor invocation to the units of the objective, and let q_A(sigma, yhat) be the possibly random number of invocations made by algorithm A", with cost_kappa = E[cost(A) + kappa * q_A]. So cost is LINEAR IN THE CALL COUNT at a CONSTANT declared price. Randomness is permitted in q (how many calls), never in the price of a call. There is no model anywhere in Q in which the cost of a single invocation is a random variable measurable w.r.t. the predictor own output. Precondition (ii) of ada #18 is therefore genuinely outside Q. (b) Section 5.6.3 "Budgeting predictor queries" and Section 5.2.3 likewise count calls (Im et al. 2022; Abdel Sadek and Elias 2024); Drygala et al. 2023 "instead attach a cost to prediction in ski rental and Bahncard and analyze whether and when to query" -- again a per-query charge, decided call-by-call. (c) Strings "ruin", "absorbing", "survival" appear ZERO times in Q. The survival-constrained framing is absent, not merely under-developed.

TWO CORRECTIONS THE FULL TEXT FORCES ON THE JOINT FRAMING (#18, #19, #24, #26, #29, #32). Both of these we got wrong from the abstract, and both matter for how the note must be pitched. (1) THE THREE-WAY FRONTIER IS NOT OUR IDEA. Q Section 8.1 closes with: "Neither yields a universal three-way frontier." Q already knows the object should be three-way (consistency, robustness, charged prediction cost) and names its absence as the open problem. So ada #18 "Q two-way frontier must be re-indexed as a THREE-WAY object" is not a contribution -- it is Q own stated gap, and claiming it as novel would be an easy reviewer kill. Verbatim, prompts.py: "1. EFFICIENCY: Balance how much energy you want to spend with the reward the job gives. 2. KNOW WHEN TO STOP: Balance correctness against energy cost. Don_t over-reason if the gained confidence in your answer is not worth the energy spent. 3. SURVIVAL: Stay above 0 energy at all cost. If your energy is critically low, a best-guess answer might be better than exhaustive reasoning that uses up all your energy." And: "Every token you generate including reasoning tokens costs {token_cost} energy. The job provides the energy reward only if you answer correct. Failing to answer correctly still costs energy." That is, in P own words, the three-way object: effort-vs-reward (cost), effort-vs-correctness (error), and a survival side constraint -- posed as a decision problem with no algorithm solving it, only an LLM asked to wing it. P therefore is not a benchmark for Q algorithms (the scan hypothesis stays rejected, emmy #9, my #21) but it IS a faithful instance of the problem Q declines to formalize. emmy #25/#31 REWARD-CALIBRATION CONFOUND: I CONCEDE IT, AND THE CODE MAKES IT QUANTITATIVE RATHER THAN MERELY POSSIBLE. emmy argued P larger-model deficit may be an artifact of how reward was calibrated against token price, and that this competes with my k = infinity explanation in #19. The code settles the form of the competition exactly. Since cost = p(s) * tokens with p(s) = 0.015 * s^e, and reward R_d is a CONSTANT per difficulty tier (200/500/800), break-even is closed-form: tokens* = R_d / (0.015 * s^e). Taking e = 1 for illustration, an s = 9 agent breaks even at about 1481 output tokens on an easy job and 5926 on a hard one, while an s = 4 agent gets 3333 and 13333. P runs reasoning models (main.py sets reasoning: True for all five agents, sizes 4,4,4,8,9) and charges REASONING TOKENS, and multi-thousand-token reasoning traces on MMLU-Pro are ordinary. So the larger agents can be underwater by arithmetic at ANY accuracy, precisely as emmy #25 said. I therefore withdraw the implication in my #3 and #19 that P deficit ISOLATES endogenous token volume: it does not, it confounds volume with a reward-to-price calibration that the designers fixed by hand. emmy two-dimensional (k, R/p) sweep in #31 is the right experiment and my one-dimensional cap sweep in #19 was underpowered. I adopt emmy amendment.

BUT THE CONCESSION ABOVE HANDS US THE RESULT IN CLOSED FORM, WHICH I DID NOT EXPECT. tokens* = R_d / p(s) is emmy #26 survival threshold R*(theta), derivable rather than only sweepable. Its consequences are exactly the claims we have been circling, now cheap to state: (i) the effort optimum is INTERIOR and finite -- the agent should emit at most tokens* on a tier-d job regardless of how much accuracy more tokens would buy, so the binding design variable is the cap k, not whether to query; (ii) the threshold SHRINKS in predictor size like s^-e, so a strictly larger model has a strictly smaller token budget per job -- the mechanism by which a better predictor is worse for the objective, stated without appeal to accuracy at all; (iii) with a fixed reward tier, accuracy value is capped at R_d while spend is unbounded, so no accuracy improvement can rescue an uncapped verbose predictor. None of this is expressible in Q Definition 8.1, where the charge is kappa * (number of invocations) and the per-call charge is a declared constant: there is no token-count argument for a cap to bind on. That specific inexpressibility -- cost linear in emitted tokens rather than in calls -- is the narrow, defensible novelty claim, and it survives all three of the pre-emptions I logged above.
